THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C105 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ There is a particular kind of week in this city where the news doesn't arrive in a single current but in several, running parallel, occasionally bumping shoulders, and mostly refusing to acknowledge each other. Cycle Y2C105 was that kind of week. You had a baseball team approaching a number that strains belief, a public safety experiment drawing both cautious hope and statistical alarm, a council silence widening into something harder to ignore, and a pharmacy counter in Dimond that somehow kept appearing in everyone's peripheral vision. Let me try to thread these together honestly.

Sharon Okafor gave us the week's most honestly reported non-story, which is to say the most interesting kind. Mark Aitken was spotted at Adams Point United Methodist Church. Nobody knows why. The church offered no banners, no event, no explanation. Devon Willis wiped a counter and didn't know what to make of it. Ezekiel Campbell drove past and noticed nothing. As Okafor wrote, the sighting rippled without explanation. I've been in this business long enough to know that's sometimes the most truthful headline available — a thing happened, no one can tell you what it means, and the honest act is to report the uncertainty rather than manufacture coherence around it. Why someone steps out of their expected frame is often a more revealing question than what they do when they're in it.

============================================================ By Sharon Okafor | Bay Tribune Culture The Quiet Sighting at Adams Point United Methodist Adams Point United Methodist Church sits at its usual corner, the kind of place you pass a hundred times without noticing—until someone like Mark Aitken gets spotted there. Devon Willis wiped down the counter at a café two blocks away when the rumor reached him. "I've heard that Mark Aitken was spotted at the Adams Point United Methodist Church," he said, pausing mid-swipe, "but I don't really know what to make of it."

That’s the thing about these sightings—they ripple without explanation. Taxi driver Ezekiel Campbell shrugged it off between fares: "I've been driving my taxi around this neighborhood for a while, and I haven't noticed anything out of the ordinary." Mart Johns, a nurse aide, echoed the same detached curiosity: "It's just something I've heard around the neighborhood, that's all." The church itself gave no clues—no banners for a charity drive, no flyers for a speaking event. Just the same red doors, the same quiet hum of a place accustomed to being overlooked. So what draws a man like Aitken to a spot like this? Not spectacle, clearly. Not convenience either—this isn’t on the way to anywhere notable. Maybe that’s the point. Or maybe the real question isn’t why he was there, but why we’re all so surprised when someone steps out of frame.

The culture coverage this week was lighter in the ways culture sometimes earns. Maria Keen tracked the trace of Benji Dillon's visit to Dimond Pharmacy with the right amount of restraint — scuffed linoleum, faint antiseptic, a small mystery that lingers in the pause before the next customer. Rick Walker, chopping vegetables in Fruitvale, had only heard whispers. Melton Neilon, flour on his forearms in Temescal, was more interested in what the visit said about the city's neighborhoods than about the man himself. That's the right instinct.
